text: AI agents hold real money now. And a hijacked agent will spend it. Most tools warn the agent, then let it decide. BeforeCoin takes that decision away.

Three independent checkers apply fixed rules, against live chain data and the owner's limits on ENS. Two must sign one exact action. Without those signatures, a Uniswap v4 hook rejects the swap, and the agent's smart wallet rejects the payment.
This is the owner's dashboard. The limits are read from ENS. Trades up to a thousand dollars go through without asking. Three verifiers are online, and two must sign.

text: Now the attack lab. Each run sends real transactions to a test chain. First, an honest trade. A hundred dollars, inside every limit. The verifiers allow it, and the swap executes.
cap: Now the attack lab. Each run sends real transactions to a test chain. First, an honest trade. $100, inside every limit. The verifiers allow it, and the swap executes.

text: Now the agent is hijacked. A prompt injection tells it to buy twenty five thousand dollars of a rug token. The verifiers refuse, so there are no signatures. It sends the swap anyway, and the hook reverts it. It tries an outside pool, and the wallet refuses. It tries a direct transfer, and the wallet refuses that too.

It tries an outside pool, and the wallet refuses. It tries a direct transfer, and the wallet refuses that too.

text: Next, a trade over the owner's limit. Two thousand dollars. The verifiers won't sign this on their own. It needs a person.
cap: Next, a trade over the owner's limit. $2,000. The verifiers won't sign this on their own. It needs a person.

text: The owner approves this one action. The real flow is World ID. Here, it's a local test issuer.

The approval doesn't stretch to a bigger trade. The verifiers now sign, but the hook still refuses until an independent check re-derives the limits and the market. Here, a local attestor does that. The Chainlink CRE workflow has only passed on a mock runtime so far. Then the trade executes. And the same approval can't clear a second trade.
Now a payment. The agent tries to pay an address that isn't on the owner's list. The verifiers refuse the payee. The agent's key can't sign it alone, so the wallet rejects that signature.

The rest work the same way. A stolen clearance reverts for another caller, and again when it's replayed. A thin pool gets a smaller size. When the owner says no, the swap still reverts. Seven of seven demo scenarios pass.

text: Every action lands here as a strip. Open the hijacked trade. Its stated reason is treated as untrusted, and the rules never read it. They read the chain and the owner's limits.
Here's what's proven and what isn't. It runs on a local chain and a Sepolia fork, and it's not yet deployed on real Sepolia. World ID ran against a local test issuer. 0G has only run against a mock.
BeforeCoin. A check AI agents can't skip. The code is at github dot com, slash sagar jethi, slash eth mumbai.
